extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, poetics, and creative writers studying Aristotle
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards (drawn from Aristotle via a critical commentary) for judging poetic works—especially tragedy and epic—focusing on character, action, moral influence, and structural unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge effect by the scheme of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moral influence of a poem should be judged... The effect resides not in the isolated parts but in the scheme of the whole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not credit a dramatist with a sentiment, theory, or purpose on the strength of some dramatic utterance removed from its proper setting; interpret words and deeds in the light of all circumstances — persons, occasion, and the end the speech/action is designed to serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of vice only by necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The representation of moral depravity finds its only excuse in ‘necessity.’ The necessity meant is the inner necessity arising out of the structure of a piece.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vice may be included only when subservient to plot/‘cogent necessity of dramatic motive’ (e.g., to allow contrasted character or to move incidents toward catastrophe). Gratuitous wickedness is forbidden (Menelaus in Euripides' Orestes cited as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary needs may override ethical rules only when constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nothing but the constraining needs of literary art are allowed to override the rules laid down for goodness of character in tragedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic exigencies can justify departures from ordinary moral expectations, but only when demanded by internal artistic structure; such exceptions should be strictly limited and justified by the work's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate poetry by its own standards, not by politics or science
rubrics_metrics.description: “The standard of correctness in poetry and politics is not the same... Poetry must be judged by its own laws, its own fundamental assumptions, and not by an alien standard.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish poetical truth from scientific or political truth; do not condemn poetic fiction simply because it contradicts historical, scientific or ethical doctrines — assess according to aesthetic and poetic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should represent the general, not the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art ought to represent the general not the particular.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal satire and attacks on particular persons are ranked as inferior art; good poetry depicts general types or representative actions rather than private scandals or individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy imitates a serious and great action (μίμησις σπουδαίας πράξεως)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift from μιμεῖται σπουδαίους (imitation of noble persons) to μίμησις σπουδαίας πράξεως (imitation of a serious/great action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on action: the subject of tragedy should be a great/serious deed whose scale and consequences justify tragic treatment; greatness of action, not merely social rank, is the key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should display heroic (elevated) goodness, not merely prosaic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “According to Aristotle, the characters portrayed by epic and tragic poetry have their basis in moral goodness; but the goodness is of the heroic order.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in epic/tragedy should be morally elevated or heroically ‘good’ in a way that arouses grandeur and imagination; ordinary, unaspiring virtue is insufficient for the aesthetic effect sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic idealization (ennobling) is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: “Defective characters ... may be ennobled (ἐπιεικεῖς ποιεῖν) by poetic treatment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets may idealize or modify character traits so that even flawed persons (e.g., Achilles' passionate temperament) conform to the conditions of ‘good’ or acceptable tragic character when poetically treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of structure and causal sequence culminating in an inevitable end
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle praises “the unity which pervades the structure of [dramas], and the closely linked sequence of parts which work up to an inevitable end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong poetic/dramatic work exhibits tight structural unity and causal linkage among episodes that drive toward an inevitable catastrophe or conclusion; inartistic structure is a common defect (one reason Aristotle censures Euripides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's moral outcomes need not conform to prosaic poetical justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “The prosaic justice, misnamed ‘poetical,’ which rewards the good man and punishes the wicked, is pronounced to be appropriate only to comedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require that tragedy end with clear moral compensation (reward/punishment); tragic form can depict the defeat of virtue or victory of villainy without thereby failing aesthetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: The end of poetry is a refined pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “He maintains consistently that the end of poetry is a refined pleasure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success of poetic art is measured by its ability to produce proper aesthetic pleasure (e.g., the blended emotions of pity and fear in tragedy), not merely by didactic moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate moral nobility with social rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance against the French critical error: σπουδαῖος denotes moral goodness not necessarily high birth; outward rank is not Aristotle’s distinguishing feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mistaking ‘illustrious by birth and position’ (social rank) for the moral/ethical quality Aristotle requires; while high rank may make great actions possible on stage, moral nobility is the intended criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test charges of moral hurtfulness by context
rubrics_metrics.description: “He suggests certain considerations whereby to test whether in a given case the censure is deserved... not to take a word or deed out of its natural context.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a poem is accused of being morally harmful, examine the work’s entire context, purposes, and structure before judging; isolated passages are insufficient evidence of overall moral wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between ethical content as a factor and the artistic end
rubrics_metrics.description: “In his praise as little as in his blame does Aristotle look to the moral content of a poem. ... The moral content of a poem or the moral character of the author ... are all-important factors in producing the total impression, but if the poet fails to produce the proper pleasure, he fails in the specific function of his art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider moral elements as contributing to the overall effect, but prioritize artistic/aesthetic success (pleasure, unity, catharsis); a poem that teaches well but fails aesthetically is still a bad poem in Aristotelian terms.
